People march in support of legalized marijuana in late January in Belem, northern Brazil. The 17-member panel worked on the report for a year and will forward it to all Latin American governments as well as the United States and the European Union, EFE said. Gaviria said the time is right to start a debate on the subject, particularly with the pragmatic openings provided by the election of President Barack Obama in the United States. "In many states in the United States, as is the case in California, they have begun to change federal policies with regard to tolerating marijuana for therapeutic purposes. Decriminalization should be accompanied by treatment for addicts and public service campaigns on abuse prevention, the commission said. "If you don't help those who are dependent, you are half way there because they are going to commit crime to get money and pay for the drug," Gaviria said. Cardoso said the group called for only the decriminalization of marijuana and not other illicit drugs because "you have to start somewhere" and it would have been unrealistic to ask the same for all drugs, EFE said. Marijuana was chosen because it is grown in all countries in the region and because it is "less harmful." The decades-old criminalization of personal consumption has failed to stop the plant's cultivation and distribution, the group said. The commission urged that all current criminal prosecution be aimed at drug cartels and organized crime and not marijuana smokers, EFE said. Zedillo did not attend the news conference but worked on the report, Cardoso said. Wednesday's recommendation was the second time in less than a week that a Latin American government official called for decriminalization. A mayor in Peru suggested Friday that the federal government legalize illicit drugs and administer them through the national health ministry. Gusto Sierra, the mayor of the Surquillo district in Lima, said a federal drug law is hypocritical because it allows maximum legally allowed quantities for some drugs and plants but doesn't say where to acquire them, the Peru 21 newspaper reported in a front-page story headlined "Say yes to drugs?" Sierra said he will take the matter up with the nation's executive branch. Zedillo served as president of Mexico from 1994-2000. Gaviria was president of Colombia from 1990-94. And Cardoso led Brazil from 1995-2002.

# Former Latin American Leaders Call for Marijuana Decriminalization

**RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN)** — Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia and Brazil issued a joint call on Wednesday for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use, urging a fundamental shift in strategy in the war on drugs, according to the Spanish news agency EFE.

The announcement came from former Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, former Colombian President Cesar Gaviria, and former Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso during a gathering in Brazil convened by the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy.

"The problem is that current policies are grounded in prejudice and fear rather than in evidence," Gaviria stated at the news conference where the commission unveiled its recommendations.

The 17-member panel spent a full year compiling the report, which will be submitted to every Latin American government, as well as to the United States and the European Union, EFE reported.

According to Gaviria, the moment is ripe for renewed debate on the issue—particularly given the pragmatic possibilities opened up by President Barack Obama's election in the United States. "In many U.S. states, California among them, there has been a shift away from federal orthodoxy toward greater tolerance of marijuana for therapeutic purposes. And in Washington, a consensus is emerging that current policy simply isn't working," Gaviria was quoted as saying.

The commission stressed that decriminalization must go hand in hand with treatment programs for addicts and public awareness campaigns focused on prevention. "If you fail to help those struggling with dependency, you've only solved half the problem—because they will still resort to crime to fund their addiction," Gaviria explained.

Cardoso clarified that the commission's recommendation was limited to marijuana rather than other illicit substances, noting that "you have to start somewhere," and that calling for blanket decriminalization across all drugs would have been unrealistic. Marijuana was selected both because it is cultivated throughout the region and because it poses comparatively fewer health risks.

The commission's report concluded that decades of criminalizing personal marijuana use have failed to curb either its cultivation or distribution. It further recommended that law enforcement resources be redirected toward dismantling drug cartels and organized crime networks, rather than targeting individual marijuana users.

Although Zedillo did not attend the news conference in person, he contributed substantially to the report, Cardoso noted.

Wednesday's announcement marked the second call for decriminalization from a Latin American official within less than a week. Just days earlier, on Friday, a mayor in Peru proposed that the national government legalize illicit drugs and oversee their distribution through the health ministry. Gustavo Sierra, mayor of Lima's Surquillo district, argued that existing drug laws are inherently contradictory, permitting legal possession limits for certain substances while failing to specify legitimate means of acquiring them—a point highlighted in a front-page story in the newspaper *Peru 21* under the headline "Say Yes to Drugs?" Sierra indicated he intends to raise the issue with the country's executive branch.

Zedillo served as President of Mexico from 1994 to 2000; Gaviria led Colombia from 1990 to 1994; and Cardoso governed Brazil from 1995 to 2002.

# Latin American Leaders Call for Marijuana Decriminalization

Three prominent former Latin American presidents have jointly called for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use, marking a significant shift in the region's approach to drug policy. Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, Cesar Gaviria of Colombia, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil made this announcement during a meeting of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, held in Brazil.

## A Call for Pragmatic Reform

Gaviria, the former Colombian president, was particularly vocal in criticizing the foundations of current drug policy, arguing that existing approaches have been shaped more by prejudice and fear than by evidence of what actually works. He suggested that the political landscape has shifted favorably for this conversation, noting that the election of Barack Obama as U.S. president has opened up a more pragmatic space for debating drug policy reform—one less encumbered by the ideological rigidity that has historically characterized U.S.-Latin American discussions on the subject.

## The Commission's Findings and Recommendations

The commission, which comprises 17 members, has been working on this issue for a full year, and its comprehensive report will be distributed not only to governments across Latin America but also to policymakers in the United States and the European Union, reflecting the international dimensions of drug policy and its enforcement.

Importantly, the commission's recommendations extend beyond simple decriminalization. The report emphasizes that any move to decriminalize marijuana must be accompanied by robust addiction treatment programs and public awareness campaigns. This holistic approach stems from a recognition that individuals struggling with addiction, if left without adequate support systems, may turn to criminal activity as a means of sustaining their drug use. The commission's stance, therefore, is not simply about relaxing enforcement but about creating a more comprehensive framework that addresses the root causes and consequences of drug dependency.

## Why Marijuana, and Why Now

Cardoso offered a clear rationale for why the commission chose to focus specifically on marijuana rather than tackling the broader universe of illicit drugs. He pointed to two key factors: first, marijuana cultivation is widespread throughout the Latin American region, making it a particularly relevant and pressing issue for local policymakers. Second, marijuana is generally regarded as less harmful than other controlled substances, positioning it as a more practical and achievable starting point for policy reform efforts.

By concentrating their recommendations on marijuana, the commission appears to be strategically building momentum for broader drug policy reform, using a substance with widespread cultivation and relatively lower perceived risk as a test case that could pave the way for more comprehensive discussions in the future.

# Latin American Leaders Call for Marijuana Decriminalization, Cite Failure of Drug War

Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil gathered at a recent meeting of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy to issue a bold call for policy reform: the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use across the region. The three ex-heads of state—representing some of the countries most devastated by drug trafficking violence—argued forcefully that current prohibition-based policies have failed not because of insufficient enforcement, but because they were built on a foundation of fear and ideology rather than scientific evidence and public health research.

The commission, which brought together 17 prominent figures from across Latin America including former presidents, intellectuals, and civil society leaders, spent the past year compiling a comprehensive report examining the consequences of the war on drugs in the region. Their conclusions are unambiguous: decades of militarized crackdowns, mass incarceration, and zero-tolerance policies have failed to curb drug consumption while fueling extraordinary levels of violence, corruption, and human rights abuses throughout Latin America.

Rather than simply calling for blanket legalization, the panel's recommendations are notably nuanced. They advocate for the decriminalization of marijuana specifically for personal use, while emphasizing that this shift must be accompanied by robust investment in addiction treatment programs and prevention campaigns aimed at reducing harm. The approach reflects a broader philosophical shift the commission is urging—one that treats drug use primarily as a public health issue rather than a criminal justice matter.

The finalized report is set to be transmitted not only to governments across Latin America but also to policymakers in the United States and the European Union, reflecting the commission's understanding that meaningful drug policy reform cannot happen in isolation. Given the transnational nature of drug trafficking and consumption, the former presidents argue that any effective solution must involve coordinated action among major consumer nations, producer countries, and transit states alike.

The timing of this push is seen as significant. Many observers within the commission and beyond believe that the Obama administration in the United States may represent a rare window of opportunity for rethinking entrenched drug policies. After decades of the U.S. exporting a hardline, supply-side approach to drug control—often pressuring Latin American nations to adopt similarly punitive measures—there is cautious optimism that Washington might now be more receptive to alternative strategies, including harm reduction and decriminalization models that have shown promise in other parts of the world.

For the former presidents involved, this initiative represents more than a policy paper; it is an attempt to fundamentally reframe a decades-long conflict that has claimed countless lives and destabilized entire nations, replacing a fear-driven paradigm with one grounded in evidence, pragmatism, and public health.

# Rio de Janeiro: The Marvelous City

Rio de Janeiro, often called the "Cidade Maravilhosa" (Marvelous City), is one of Brazil's most iconic destinations and a symbol of the country's vibrant culture. Located along the southeastern coast of Brazil, Rio combines stunning natural beauty with rich history and dynamic urban life.

## Natural Wonders

The city is famous for its dramatic landscape, where lush green mountains meet pristine beaches and the sparkling Atlantic Ocean. The iconic Christ the Redeemer statue stands atop Corcovado Mountain, overlooking the city with arms outstretched, and has become one of the most recognized monuments in the world. Nearby, Sugarloaf Mountain offers cable car rides with breathtaking panoramic views of Rio's coastline, forests, and urban sprawl.

## Beaches and Lifestyle

Copacabana and Ipanema are perhaps the most famous beaches in Rio, drawing both locals (known as "Cariocas") and tourists from around the globe. These beaches aren't just about sunbathing—they represent a way of life centered on outdoor activities, volleyball, football, and socializing along the beachfront promenades.

## Culture and Celebration

Rio de Janeiro is world-renowned for its Carnival celebrations, held annually before Lent. The event features elaborate parades, samba schools competing with dazzling costumes and choreography, and street parties that attract millions of visitors. This celebration showcases Brazil's rich Afro-Brazilian heritage and the infectious energy of samba music.

## Historical Significance

As Brazil's capital until 1960 (when Brasília took over that role), Rio holds significant historical importance. The city features colonial architecture, historic churches, and museums that tell the story of Brazil's colonial past, independence, and development into a modern nation.

## Challenges and Resilience

Like many major cities, Rio faces challenges including economic inequality, visible in the contrast between wealthy neighborhoods and favelas (informal settlements) that climb the hillsides. Despite these challenges, the city continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience and creativity, with community initiatives and cultural programs helping to address social issues.

Rio de Janeiro remains a testament to Brazil's diversity, natural splendor, and cultural richness, continuing to captivate visitors with its unique blend of urban energy and breathtaking landscapes.

# Former Latin American Leaders Renew Push for Marijuana Decriminalization

**By CNN Staff**

A coalition of former Latin American presidents has issued a renewed call for the decriminalization of marijuana and a broader rethinking of drug policy across the Americas, arguing that decades of prohibition-focused strategies have failed to curb violence, corruption, and drug use while devastating communities across the region.

The group, which includes former heads of state from Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil, released a joint statement urging governments to shift away from punitive approaches and toward policies rooted in public health, harm reduction, and human rights.

"The war on drugs has been lost," the statement read, echoing language used by similar commissions over the past decade. "We have spent enormous resources fighting a war that has not reduced consumption, has fueled organized crime, and has filled our prisons with nonviolent offenders, disproportionately from poor and marginalized communities."

Among the most vocal advocates has been former Mexican President Vicente Fox, who has long argued that legalization — rather than criminalization — would undercut the financial power of drug cartels. Former Colombian President César Gaviria, who has been part of similar commissions in the past, including the Global Commission on Drug Policy, reiterated that prohibition has largely benefited criminal organizations rather than curbing narcotics trade.

"Every year we don't act, we hand more power and profit to traffickers," Gaviria said in remarks accompanying the statement. "Decriminalization is not about promoting drug use — it's about taking the market out of the hands of criminals and treating addiction as a health issue, not a criminal one."

The former leaders pointed to models already implemented in Uruguay, which became the first country in the world to fully legalize marijuana production, sale, and consumption in 2013, and in several U.S. states, as evidence that regulated markets can reduce black-market activity without triggering spikes in usage.

They also emphasized that current drug laws have had a disproportionate impact on the poor, noting that low-level offenders — often young men from disadvantaged backgrounds — bear the brunt of enforcement while high-level traffickers frequently evade justice.

Critics of decriminalization, however, argue that loosening drug laws could send the wrong message to younger generations and potentially increase consumption rates. Some conservative lawmakers across the region have pushed back against the proposals, warning that decriminalization could complicate relations with the United States, particularly given past tensions over drug enforcement cooperation.

Still, public opinion in several Latin American countries has shifted in recent years, with growing support for alternative approaches to drug policy, particularly regarding marijuana. Mexico's Supreme Court itself ruled in past cases that outright prohibition of recreational marijuana use was unconstitutional, adding legal momentum to the broader debate even as comprehensive legislation has stalled in the country's Congress.

The former presidents' coalition says it plans to continue pressing regional governments and international bodies, including the United Nations, to reconsider drug classification systems and invest more heavily in treatment and prevention programs rather than incarceration.

"This is not a partisan issue," the statement concluded. "It is about recognizing reality and choosing policies that actually work."

*This is a developing story.*

Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, César Gaviria of Colombia, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil—co-chairs of the Global Commission on Drug Policy—delivered a joint statement urging governments across the region and beyond to abandon punitive, enforcement-heavy approaches in favor of policies rooted in public health, human rights, and evidence-based regulation.

The statement arrives against a backdrop of continued cartel violence in Mexico, prison crises in Brazil, and persistent trafficking routes through Colombia—all countries the three leaders once governed. # Latin America's Growing Movement to Rethink Drug Policy

*A wave of political voices across the region is pushing for cannabis decriminalization, arguing that decades of prohibition have failed to curb violence while filling prisons with nonviolent offenders.*

For over a decade, a growing chorus of Latin American leaders—many speaking out after leaving office—has called for fundamental reforms to drug policy, with marijuana decriminalization emerging as a central demand. Their argument is straightforward: the war on drugs has produced staggering violence, corruption, and mass incarceration without meaningfully reducing consumption or trafficking.

## A Regional Reckoning

The push gained significant momentum in 2009 when former presidents Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil, César Gaviria of Colombia, and Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico co-authored a report through the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy. The document argued that prohibition-focused strategies had failed catastrophically.

"The available evidence indicates that the war on drugs is a war that has been lost," the commission stated bluntly, calling instead for treating drug use as a public health issue rather than a criminal matter.

Gaviria, who led Colombia during some of the bloodiest years of the cartel wars, has been particularly vocal. "We have to break the taboo and take a fresh look at the drug issue," he said in later remarks. "Prohibition has not worked. It's time to think about alternatives, starting with marijuana."

## Uruguay's Landmark Experiment

Uruguay became a global testing ground when it fully legalized marijuana in 2013 under President José Mujica, making it the first country to regulate the entire cannabis market—from cultivation to sale.

Mujica, a former guerrilla fighter turned head of state known for his plainspoken philosophy, framed the decision in pragmatic terms. "Someone has to be the first," he remarked at the time. "This isn't about promoting marijuana use. It's about taking the business away from narco-trafficking."

He later expanded on the reasoning behind the policy: "We're not doing this because we think drug use is good. We're doing it because prohibition has handed an enormous, profitable business to organized crime, and that has cost us far more in blood and institutional damage than the drug itself."

## Mexico's Shifting Stance

In Mexico, where cartel violence has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives, former President Vicente Fox became an outspoken advocate for legalization after leaving office in 2006.

"Prohibition doesn't work," Fox said in various interviews over the years. "Look at what happened with alcohol in the United States—the mafias grew rich, violence increased, and eventually the policy was abandoned as a failure. We're repeating the same mistake with marijuana, except the cost in Mexican lives has been far higher."

His successor, Felipe Calderón, who launched Mexico's militarized crackdown on cartels in 2006, later expressed more nuanced views on reform, acknowledging that "we need a serious, open conversation about alternatives, including regulated markets, because the current model is unsustainable."

## The Colombian Perspective

Colombia, long ground zero for the drug war's most brutal chapters, has produced some of the region's most persistent reform advocates. Former President Juan Manuel Santos, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016 for negotiating peace with FARC rebels, has argued that drug policy and conflict resolution are inseparable issues.

"For fifty years, we fought a war that filled our cemeteries and emptied our public trust," Santos said. "Meanwhile, consumption in the countries demanding these drugs continued to rise. At some point, you must ask whether the tool you're using is the right one."

## Arguments Against the Status Quo

Proponents of reform consistently make several arguments:

- **Violence reduction**: Removing marijuana from the black market could weaken cartel revenue streams, some of which rely heavily on cannabis trafficking to the United States and Europe.
- **Prison overcrowding**: Latin American prisons are disproportionately filled with low-level, nonviolent drug offenders, often from impoverished communities.
- **Public health framing**: Advocates argue that treating addiction as a medical issue rather than a criminal one yields better outcomes.
- **Economic opportunity**: Legal cannabis markets could generate tax revenue and create jobs, as seen in parts of the United States and Canada.

## Persistent Obstacles

Despite high-profile advocacy, implementation remains uneven across the region. Political resistance, concerns about public health messaging, and pressure from international drug treaties have slowed broader adoption. Some conservative and religious constituencies continue to view decriminalization as sending the wrong message to younger generations.

Additionally, critics note that decriminalizing marijuana alone does little to address the more lucrative and violent trade in cocaine, which remains central to organized crime's influence in countries like Colombia, Peru, and Bolivia.

## Looking Ahead

As more countries—including several U.S. states and Canada—move toward regulated cannabis markets, pressure is mounting on Latin American governments to reconsider decades-old prohibition frameworks. For former leaders like Mujica, Gaviria, and Fox, the calculus remains simple: policies should be judged by their results, not their intentions.

"We tried prohibition for fifty years," Gaviria has said. "It's time to try something else."

---

*This article reflects statements and positions attributed to various former Latin American heads of state regarding drug policy reform. Policies and political circumstances continue to evolve across the region.*

The former leaders highlighted the growing divide within the United States itself, where a majority of states have now legalized marijuana for medical or recreational use, even as it remains classified as a Schedule I substance under federal law. That contradiction, advocates argue, has created confusion for law enforcement, banking institutions, and consumers alike, while fueling calls for Washington to formally reconcile state and federal policy.

Supporters of reform argue that legalization has generated tax revenue, reduced arrests for low-level possession, and allowed for regulated markets that undercut illicit dealers. Critics, however, caution that loosening restrictions further could increase youth access and dependency, and they warn against assuming success in one country will translate globally.

## Peru's Ongoing Debate

The discussion also turned to Peru, where lawmakers and civil society groups have been engaged in their own contentious debate over cannabis policy. Peru has permitted medical marijuana use in limited circumstances, but proposals to expand access—or to move toward broader decriminalization—have met resistance from conservative lawmakers and law enforcement officials wary of the country's history with coca cultivation and drug trafficking networks.

Advocates in Peru argue that a more permissive medical marijuana framework could benefit patients with epilepsy, chronic pain, and other conditions, while also opening the door to economic opportunities in a regulated cannabis industry. Opponents counter that Peru's institutions are not yet equipped to manage expanded legalization without strengthening regulatory oversight first.

## A Broader Regional Reckoning

The former presidents' remarks come amid a broader reassessment across the Americas of drug policies rooted in the U.S.-led "war on drugs" launched decades ago. Several Latin American nations have experimented with decriminalization, alternative sentencing, and harm-reduction programs, often citing the toll of drug-related violence on their societies.

"The war on drugs, as it has been fought, has cost too many lives and filled too many prisons without reducing the availability of drugs," another former leader said. "We owe it to future generations to try a different approach—one based on evidence, health, and human rights."

The group called on the United Nations and national governments to revisit international drug treaties, arguing that a more flexible, health-centered framework would better address the realities of addiction and trafficking in the 21st century.

As marijuana legalization debates continue to unfold from statehouses in the U.S. to the halls of Peru's Congress, the former presidents' intervention underscores a growing international appetite for rethinking policies that have shaped the drug war for more than 50 years. Whether that appetite translates into coordinated policy change remains, for now, an open question.
